explanation: A browser asks a server for a resource using HTTP, the Hypertext Transfer Protocol. The request supplies a method, target, headers and sometimes a body. The response supplies a status, headers and content. HTTPS carries this exchange inside TLS. The browser then interprets HTML as document structure, CSS as presentation and JavaScript as behavior. The Document Object Model (DOM) is the tree of page nodes that scripts can read or change.

A URL names a scheme, host, effective port, path, query and optional fragment. In https://shop.example:8443/cart?id=6#total, the request carries the path and query; the fragment stays in the browser. An origin is the tuple (scheme, exact hostname, effective port). HTTPS’s default port is 443. Thus https://shop.example/a and https://shop.example:443/b share an origin; a subdomain, HTTP, or port 8443 changes it. The Same-Origin Policy (SOP) restricts cross-origin access to documents and response data.

A classic external script runs with the including document’s origin, even when downloaded from a different host. An iframe creates a separate document whose origin follows its own loaded URL, subject to sandboxing. Including another party’s script therefore gives that code access to the page’s authority. A cross-origin image or form can initiate a request while SOP restricts reading the returned data. Request transmission and response reading are separate browser decisions.

A server uses Set-Cookie to store state in the browser. A session cookie usually contains an unpredictable identifier referring to server-side login state. A cookie without Domain is host-only. Domain=example.com can cover example.com and its subdomains when set by an eligible host such as shop.example.com. A host can set an eligible parent domain, but an unrelated domain or public suffix is rejected. The acceptance check happens when setting the cookie; the delivery check happens on each later request.

For delivery, the destination host must match, the request path must path-match, and the remaining attribute rules must permit sending. Path=/cart matches /cart and /cart/items, with the path-segment boundary rule; it does not match /cartoon. Cookies have no port field. Secure restricts sending to secure transport. HttpOnly blocks JavaScript cookie API access while permitting eligible HTTP requests to carry the cookie. Path scopes delivery and supplies no reliable isolation from scripts within the same origin.

SameSite uses a site boundary, which groups hosts under a registrable domain and considers scheme in modern browsers. Strict generally withholds the cookie on cross-site requests. Lax permits some top-level safe navigations. SameSite=None permits cross-site use and requires Secure in modern browsers. Credentials and browser privacy settings also affect requests. A sibling subdomain can be cross-origin while remaining same-site. A cookie can be removed with matching name/domain/path and an expired lifetime. The __Host- prefix requires Secure, Path=/ and no Domain attribute, producing a host-bound cookie.
example: A response from https://shop.example.com/account sets sid with Path=/account; Secure; HttpOnly and no Domain. A later HTTPS request to shop.example.com:8443/account/orders can carry it: the host and path match, Secure is satisfied, and cookies ignore ports. A request to api.example.com/account lacks this host-only cookie. Apply SameSite and request-credential rules separately when the request context crosses sites.

questions.prompt: A page at https://shop.example.com includes a classic script from https://cdn.example.net and an iframe from that same CDN. Which origin supplies each resource’s document authority?
questions.hint: Follow whether the resource becomes code in the existing document or a separate document.
questions.answer: The classic script executes with the shop document’s https://shop.example.com origin. The iframe is a separate document at https://cdn.example.net. SOP restricts access between the two documents unless a permitted sharing mechanism applies.

questions.prompt: A host-only Secure cookie for shop.example.com has Path=/pay. Compare HTTPS requests to shop.example.com/pay/confirm, shop.example.com/payroll, and api.example.com/pay. Assume SameSite and credential settings permit sending.
questions.hint: Check destination host, then the path-segment match, then secure transport.
questions.answer: The first request matches host and path and uses HTTPS, so the cookie is eligible. /payroll fails the path boundary after /pay. api.example.com fails the host-only condition. Ports do not enter the cookie scope test.

explanation: A review page needs to display a customer’s words. A search page needs to place a search value into a database lookup. In both cases an application receives data and chooses how another component will interpret it. Injection happens when attacker-controlled characters gain the structure or execution role reserved for application code.

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) runs attacker-controlled code with the vulnerable page’s origin. Stored XSS saves the input in a record, such as a review, that later reaches readers. Reflected XSS returns a value from the current request in an executable context. DOM-based XSS occurs when page JavaScript reads attacker-controlled data and passes it to an unsafe browser sink. A sink is the operation that consumes the data, such as an HTML parser or code evaluator.

Once script runs in the account page’s origin, it can read accessible DOM data and issue actions with that page’s authority. An HttpOnly cookie keeps its value out of JavaScript cookie APIs; browser requests can still attach that cookie. HTTPS protects delivery to the genuine site while the site’s vulnerable content supplies the execution path. The repair belongs at the input-to-interpreter boundary.

Use text-node operations for plain text. When a value belongs in HTML, an attribute, a URL or JavaScript, apply the defense appropriate to that exact context; their parsing rules differ. A well-maintained sanitizer can permit a restricted set of markup where rich content is required. A Content Security Policy (CSP) constrains script and resource execution, such as limiting script-src to approved origins and nonces. Its value depends on which code the policy trusts and whether the execution path is covered.

Structured Query Language (SQL) injection reaches the server’s database query parser. Concatenating an untrusted name into query text can allow punctuation and operators to alter its parse tree. Parentheses, quote context, comment rules and operator precedence determine the resulting query. A database executes the parsed query with the application account’s permissions, so excessive database rights increase possible damage.

A prepared statement sends a fixed SQL structure with placeholders and binds input as parameter values. For SELECT price FROM stock WHERE sku = ?, an arbitrary sku string stays a value for that one placeholder. Dynamic identifiers, such as a selected column name, usually need an explicit allowlist because ordinary value parameters do not stand for query syntax. Least-privilege database accounts limit the resources any successful query can reach. Browser output handling and database parameter binding act at their respective interpreters.
example: An inventory service binds a user’s product name to a prepared WHERE name = ? query. It then displays the returned name using a DOM text node. Parameter binding keeps the supplied name inside a database value; text insertion keeps the returned characters inside page text. Each defense follows the data into the component that will interpret it.

questions.prompt: A site changes its database lookups to prepared statements. It still displays stored review text by assigning that text to innerHTML. Explain the remaining execution path and a suitable repair.
questions.hint: Name the component that receives the stored text after the database lookup finishes.
questions.answer: A stored review can still reach the browser’s HTML interpreter through innerHTML and create an XSS path. Use textContent for plain reviews, or a carefully maintained markup sanitizer if a restricted rich-text format is required. The prepared query protects the separate database parsing boundary.

questions.prompt: A site has script-src limited to its own origin, but lets users upload executable JavaScript at that origin. What dependency makes the policy weak?
questions.hint: Follow where the policy’s permitted code can originate.
questions.answer: The policy trusts script served by the site’s origin. User-controlled executable uploads on that origin can supply permitted script, so the allowlist includes attacker-controlled code. Upload handling, content types, execution isolation and the CSP trust set must be designed together.

explanation: A logged-in account page lets its user change a delivery address. A session cookie identifies the account. If an attacker can cause that browser to submit a chosen address and the server accepts the request, the account changes even though the attacker never learned the session value. Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) exploits the browser’s role as a credential-carrying deputy.

Trace a CSRF case through its inputs: an action the attacker can induce, attacker-chosen action data, an active victim session, and credentials that the browser actually sends. The request method, encoding, site relationship, cookie SameSite policy and request credential mode all matter. State-changing GET handlers can expose actions to ordinary link or image loading. Sensitive operations should use appropriate methods plus explicit intent checks.

A synchronizer token is an unpredictable value associated with the session that the legitimate page can supply and the server verifies for an action. It must reach the correct validation point and resist attacker acquisition. Origin validation compares a browser-supplied request origin with a trusted allowlist; missing or unexpected values require an explicit policy. A carefully designed SameSite cookie policy reduces cross-site credential delivery. These controls protect different stages and can work together.

CORS, Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, grants a script permission to read selected cross-origin response data. A server can return Access-Control-Allow-Origin for a specific requesting origin. Credentialed reading also requires the matching credential permission; a wildcard origin does not grant credentialed sharing. Some methods, headers or content types require a preflight request. Simple cross-origin requests, such as eligible form submissions, can reach the server without that preflight.

The Same-Origin Policy and CORS govern browser access to response information. The server’s CSRF and authorization checks decide whether an action should happen. An attacker can benefit from an accepted action while the browser hides the reply. Conversely, a permitted cross-origin reader still needs the application’s authorization for the requested resource.

For window messaging, postMessage lets a sender specify an intended target origin. The receiver checks event.origin, the expected source window and the message structure before acting. A correct origin check identifies the communicating document; authorization then decides which actions that document may request. XSS within a trusted page can use the page’s readable tokens and authority, which makes safe page execution part of the larger action boundary.
example: A picture-hosting page induces a form POST to a billing site. Assume the browser sends the billing session cookie and the handler accepts a new address with no token or origin check. The change can succeed even while SOP hides the billing response from the picture page. Adding a session-bound token that the picture page cannot obtain gives the billing handler a concrete intent check.

questions.prompt: An attacker page can submit a simple cross-origin POST, but CORS prevents it from reading the reply. The target accepts the victim’s cookie and updates the account without a CSRF token. Can the update occur? Explain the stages.
questions.hint: Separate delivering the request, validating the action and exposing the response.
questions.answer: Yes. The browser can deliver an eligible simple POST with the permitted credentials. The target then accepts the action using the session. CORS can withhold the reply from attacker JavaScript after the state change. The target needs an action-intent check such as a correctly validated session-bound token and an appropriate origin/cookie policy.

questions.prompt: A cookie has SameSite=Strict. A request comes from a compromised sibling subdomain over the same scheme. Which boundary must you evaluate before relying on Strict as the action defense?
questions.hint: Compare origin and registrable-domain site boundaries.
questions.answer: A sibling subdomain has a different origin but can share the same site. SameSite=Strict governs cross-site delivery, so a same-site sibling request may remain eligible. The server still needs its intended origin and action checks, and the actual request’s credential behavior must be traced.

explanation: A login server needs a repeatable way to check a submitted secret. At enrollment it chooses a fresh salt s and work settings c, then computes v = F(p, s, c), where p is the password and F is a suitable password-hashing function. The account record stores s, c and verifier v. On login it computes F(p′, s, c) for the submitted password p′ and compares the result with v. A successful check can establish a session; authorization then governs the resources that session may use.

A salt is public per-record data. Fresh independent salts make equal passwords produce different verifiers with overwhelming probability and force candidate calculations to depend on the particular record. An attacker who copies the database also gets those salts. Their security role is to separate work among records and defeat reusable precomputed password tables for the unsalted function.

Password-hashing functions such as bcrypt or scrypt deliberately make each guess costly; memory-hard designs add memory demands. Work settings choose the cost on the specified implementation and hardware. Fast general-purpose hashes make large guessing campaigns inexpensive. The user’s password distribution also matters: common words, reuse and predictable alterations give an attacker a productive guess order. Length and unpredictability increase the useful candidate space.

In an online attack, each guess reaches the service, where rate limits and additional factors can constrain it. In an offline attack, copied verifiers let the attacker test candidates on its own hardware. Service-side login limits therefore act on a different path from a database-leak guessing campaign. Protecting the record, increasing each guess’s cost and improving password choices address the inputs to that campaign.

Let D be the number of candidate passwords, N the number of independently salted accounts, t seconds per complete candidate/account calculation, and W identical independent workers. Testing every candidate against every record requires ND calculations. Ideal elapsed time is T = NDt/W seconds. This assumes fixed per-calculation cost and ideal scheduling; actual parallelism may be limited by memory, hardware and overhead. Finding a particular password earlier in the list changes the stopping time. Fig. 2 supplies a companion case: the mean search for one account whose secret is uniformly selected from 2^h candidates, where h is bits of uncertainty. About 2^(h−1) distinct guesses are needed on average. Its per-worker cost is entered in microseconds (1 µs = 10⁻⁶ seconds); increasing parallel workers increases the modeled aggregate guess rate.

After authentication, the session identifier becomes valuable evidence. It should be unpredictable, protected in transport, constrained by suitable cookie attributes, expired as appropriate and invalidated on logout or compromise. Multifactor authentication combines evidence categories; a password plus a second password still belongs to the knowledge category. Recovery and enrollment paths need comparable care because they can grant the same account access.
example: For 60 independently salted accounts, 40,000 candidates, 0.012 seconds per complete calculation and 8 ideal workers, the full campaign costs 2,400,000 calculations. T = 60 × 40,000 × 0.012 / 8 = 3,600 seconds, or one hour. This is a work estimate for the stated candidate list and hardware, rather than a claim about a particular real password.

questions.prompt: A stolen database contains 25 distinct salts and verifiers. An attacker tests 12,000 candidates against every account at 0.02 seconds per computation on five ideal workers. Find computation count and elapsed time.
questions.hint: Count candidate/account pairs, then multiply by seconds and divide by workers.
questions.answer: ND = 25 × 12,000 = 300,000 complete computations. Ideal time is 300,000 × 0.02 / 5 = 1,200 seconds, or 20 minutes. The model assumes the entire list is tested for every account and that five workers sustain the stated per-worker cost.

questions.prompt: Two accounts chose the same password. Their records use fresh independent salts. Explain how this changes precomputation and what a database thief still needs to do.
questions.hint: Name the inputs to F for each record.
questions.answer: Each salt changes the candidate calculation, so one precomputed unsalted result cannot be reused as the verifier for both records. The thief has each public salt and settings, and can still compute F(candidate, salt, settings) and compare with that account’s verifier. Guess cost and password predictability determine the remaining effort.

explanation: Single Sign-On (SSO) lets several services rely on one identity provider (IdP) to authenticate users. The destination is a service provider (SP), also called a relying party in identity systems. The browser participates in redirects or message delivery. In the signed-token model, the IdP authenticates the user, creates protected identity claims, and the SP verifies that evidence before creating its own session.

A signature check requires a key belonging to a trusted issuer. The SP also checks the intended audience, validity times and binding to the current login request, including the protocol’s nonce or other request-correlation values. A signed claim for one service has an intended recipient; that recipient check keeps it from becoming a general login pass. The exact exchanges depend on the federation protocol. SAML means Security Assertion Markup Language; OpenID Connect supplies authentication on top of the OAuth 2.0 authorization framework.

A common IdP can centralize strong authentication and reduce repeated password entry and reuse. It also becomes a shared availability, privacy and signing-key dependency. Several services may fail together during an IdP outage, and a compromised trusted signing key can undermine the evidence those services accept. Each SP still decides what an authenticated account may do.

A passkey is a public-key credential associated with a relying party. During registration, an authenticator creates or protects a key pair and the service records the credential’s public key with the account. The private key remains under the protection of the authenticator or passkey provider. A local PIN or biometric check can authorize its use. A synced passkey may be securely copied through its provider’s system, making that provider’s account and recovery protections part of the trust model.

During authentication the service supplies a fresh challenge. The authenticator signs an assertion that binds the response to the relying party and the browser exchange. The service verifies the signature with the stored public key and checks the expected challenge, relying-party identifier, origin and required user-presence or user-verification flags. The browser/authenticator protocol restricts credential use to the relying party’s scope, giving phishing resistance when the complete validation succeeds.

WebAuthn means Web Authentication and defines the browser interface. FIDO2 combines WebAuthn with authenticator protocols. A passkey’s local unlock value authorizes key use on the device; the service verifies the resulting public-key proof. Enrollment, account linking, lost-device recovery and alternate login methods can all lead to the same account, so their trust checks belong in a complete authentication design.
example: An IdP signs a token with audience “library” during a library login. Payroll receives a copied token with a valid signature. Its audience check rejects the token for payroll. In a passkey login, replaying yesterday’s assertion fails the fresh challenge check even when that old signature still verifies over yesterday’s assertion.

questions.prompt: A service verifies an IdP token’s signature but accepts any audience and request nonce. Which checks should it complete, and what does each establish?
questions.hint: Identify issuer, destination, time and current login exchange.
questions.answer: It must use the trusted issuer’s key and validate the expected issuer, its own audience, permitted validity period and the federation protocol’s current-request binding such as the expected nonce. These establish who issued the claims, which service they target, when they apply and which login they answer. Authorization follows after authentication.

questions.prompt: A service stores a passkey public key. What additional values must a successful login assertion be checked against, and why does a fresh challenge matter?
questions.hint: Follow the registration binding and this login’s browser exchange.
questions.answer: The service checks the signature with the registered key, the expected challenge, relying-party identifier, allowed origin, and required presence/verification flags under WebAuthn’s rules. The fresh challenge binds the proof to this authentication attempt and prevents an old assertion from serving as a new proof.

title: Email domain authentication
heading: Follow the peer, envelope, signature and visible author separately
problem: two aligned authentication routes that can support a message’s visible From domain.
figureSvg: <svg xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg' role='img' aria-labelledby='email-auth-title' viewBox='0 0 720 360'><title id='email-auth-title'>SPF and DKIM routes to an aligned DMARC pass</title><defs><marker id='email-auth-arrow' markerWidth='8' markerHeight='8' refX='7' refY='4' orient='auto'><path d='M0 0 L8 4 L0 8 Z' fill='#176a70'/></marker></defs><g font-family='system-ui, sans-serif' fill='#17343d'><text x='360' y='28' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Visible From: billing@shop.example</text><rect x='20' y='65' width='310' height='120' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='175.0' y='108.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>SPF route</text><text x='175.0' y='130.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>peer IP authorized by envelope domain</text><text x='175.0' y='152.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>AND envelope domain aligns</text><rect x='390' y='65' width='310' height='120' rx='8' fill='#fff3dd' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='545.0' y='108.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>DKIM route</text><text x='545.0' y='130.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>signature verifies for d= domain</text><text x='545.0' y='152.0' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>AND signing domain aligns</text><path d='M175 185 L320 245' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#email-auth-arrow)'/><path d='M545 185 L400 245' fill='none' stroke='#176a70' stroke-width='2' marker-end='url(#email-auth-arrow)'/><rect x='280' y='245' width='160' height='65' rx='8' fill='#edf4f1' stroke='#176a70'/><text x='360.0' y='271.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Either route</text><text x='360.0' y='293.5' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>DMARC pass</text><text x='360' y='342' text-anchor='middle' font-size='16'>Authentication result → alignment → published policy → receiver handling</text></g></svg>
explanation: An incoming message names several identities. The SMTP envelope sender receives delivery reports. The visible From header claims the author shown to the reader. A DKIM signature names a signing domain. The receiver also observes the connecting SMTP peer’s IP address. Domain-authentication checks begin by selecting the identity they actually evaluate.

Sender Policy Framework (SPF) evaluates the connecting peer IP against the envelope-sender domain’s DNS TXT policy, or the HELO identity in applicable cases. Mechanisms such as ip4 and include can match that IP. The matching mechanism’s qualifier gives pass (+), fail (-), softfail (~), or neutral (?). A final -all produces fail when no earlier mechanism matched. The receiver then uses that evidence in its handling policy.

DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM) signs selected message headers and body data. In a DKIM-Signature header, d= names the signing domain and s= selects a key. The lookup is selector._domainkey.signing-domain. The receiver retrieves the public key, checks the covered body hash bh= and verifies b= under the declared algorithm and canonicalization rules. Coverage fields such as h= identify signed headers. The evidence applies to those covered data under the signing domain.

Domain-based Message Authentication, Reporting, and Conformance (DMARC) connects a passing identity with the visible From domain through alignment. Let S mean SPF passes, Aₛ mean its envelope domain aligns, D mean a DKIM signature passes, and Aᴅ mean that signature’s domain aligns. Then DMARC pass = (S AND Aₛ) OR (D AND Aᴅ). Strict alignment requires exact domain agreement. Relaxed alignment can accept subdomains sharing the applicable organizational domain.

The receiver looks up the visible From domain’s DMARC policy at _dmarc.domain, applying the protocol’s fallback rules where relevant. A policy can request none, quarantine or reject for failures, and rua can request aggregate reporting. Authentication, alignment, requested handling and the receiver’s final disposition are separate stages. A domain authorized to send mail can still send harmful content, so domain evidence supports spoofing assessment alongside content and reputation checks.

Forwarding changes the connecting peer IP and can therefore break SPF for the original envelope identity. DKIM can survive when the covered data stay intact; a mailing list’s body or header edits can break it. A valid signature can also accompany a replay. Each receiving server prepends a Received header, placing the newest hop first. The current receiver directly observed its immediate peer; older trace lines depend on trust in the systems that supplied them.

Spam filtering combines evidence about content, behavior, reputation and authenticated domains. Provider controls and legal accountability address other stages of abuse. A protocol pass establishes its specific identity claim, while the user-facing safety decision also depends on what the message asks the recipient to do.
example: A message displays From: billing@shop.example, uses envelope bounce@mailer.example, and carries a valid DKIM signature with d=shop.example. SPF passes for mailer.example but lacks alignment with shop.example. The exactly aligned DKIM pass supplies the DMARC passing route. If a forwarder later changes the signed body, DKIM may fail and the receiver must recompute the available routes.

questions.prompt: Visible From is alerts@example.com. SPF passes for bounce@dispatch.example.net. DKIM passes with d=mail.example.com. With relaxed alignment, does DMARC pass? What changes under strict alignment?
questions.hint: Compute pass and alignment together for each route; use the visible From domain as the comparison target.
questions.answer: Under relaxed alignment, the DKIM signing domain mail.example.com shares organizational domain example.com with visible From, so the DKIM route passes and aligns. SPF’s example.net identity is unrelated. Under strict alignment the DKIM domain differs from example.com, so neither route supplies an aligned pass and DMARC fails, assuming no other passing signature.

questions.prompt: A forwarder preserves signed message data but sends from a new IP. Explain which authentication input changes and which can remain valid.
questions.hint: SPF follows the current SMTP peer; DKIM follows covered message data.
questions.answer: The next receiver observes the forwarder’s IP, which may fall outside the original envelope domain’s SPF policy. DKIM can still verify if the signature and all required covered data remain valid. The receiver then tests alignment of any passing identity with visible From and applies its handling policy.

POP3 retrieves; HTTPS supports webmail.</text></g></svg>
explanation: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) submits and relays mail. The sending server uses the recipient domain’s DNS mail-exchanger (MX) records to locate a destination. Internet Message Access Protocol (IMAP) gives a client mailbox access and synchronized state. Post Office Protocol version 3 (POP3) supports message retrieval for local access. Webmail puts an HTTP application in front of mail operations. These protocols serve different parts of the message’s journey.

STARTTLS upgrades an existing connection. An SMTP client sends EHLO, reads the server’s capabilities, requests STARTTLS, completes a TLS handshake on the same connection and port, then begins the protected SMTP exchange with a new EHLO. Implicit TLS runs the TLS handshake immediately after TCP connects, before mail commands. Common ports are SMTP relay 25, submission 587 with STARTTLS or 465 with implicit TLS, IMAP 143 with upgrade or 993 implicit, and POP3 110 with STLS upgrade or 995 implicit.

With opportunistic TLS, delivery may fall back to plaintext if TLS is unavailable. An active intermediary who strips an unprotected STARTTLS advertisement can trigger that allowed fallback. A sender that requires authenticated TLS instead stops or defers delivery when its required endpoint checks fail. The sender’s acceptance policy determines whether an unusable protected connection becomes a delivery failure or plaintext exposure.

Each TLS session ends at its two peers. A mail server decrypts the incoming connection to process the message and creates another connection for the next hop. Encrypting all links therefore places those servers inside the plaintext trust boundary. End-to-end message encryption instead protects the message before submission and lets intermediate servers relay the resulting encrypted object.

Hybrid message encryption uses a fresh symmetric content key K to protect message M, producing ciphertext C = Enc_K(M). It protects K for the recipient using the recipient’s authentic public key, producing a wrapped key E. The recipient’s private key recovers K, and K opens C. Real formats specify authenticated encryption, key wrapping and the exact protected fields. A sender’s private signing key can separately sign covered message data; the recipient verifies that signature with the sender’s authentic public signing key.

Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) traditionally uses user endorsements and local trust policy for public-key bindings. Secure/Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions (S/MIME) uses a certificate infrastructure. Both require correct public-key distribution, private-key protection, revocation and usable recovery. Routing metadata and uncovered headers can remain visible. Endpoints that decrypt the object can read it, and content filtering must operate where the content is accessible.
example: An organization encrypts each SMTP hop and stores ordinary mail on its servers. Those servers can process message content because they terminate TLS. If a sender encrypts the message object for the recipient before SMTP submission, the relays carry that object while still observing routing information, timing and size. Each claim follows the endpoint at which its encryption ends.

questions.prompt: An intermediary removes STARTTLS from an SMTP capability reply. Compare a sender permitting plaintext fallback with one requiring authenticated TLS before transmission.
questions.hint: Identify the connection each policy accepts before releasing mail content.
questions.answer: The opportunistic sender may continue in plaintext under its fallback policy, exposing that hop’s content. The sender requiring authenticated TLS stops or defers when acceptable TLS cannot be established, preserving confidentiality at an availability cost. Endpoint identity validation is part of the required TLS policy.

questions.prompt: For an encrypted and signed message from Ada to Ben, identify which keys let Ben recover content and verify the sender, and which assumption connects those keys to people.
questions.hint: Separate the recipient’s encryption role from the sender’s signing role.
questions.answer: Ben uses his private decryption key to recover the content key, then that symmetric key to open the protected content. He uses Ada’s authentic public signing key to verify her signature over the covered data. Correct identity-to-public-key bindings, established through the chosen trust system, connect those cryptographic roles to Ada and Ben.

explanation: A company exposes a public website while keeping its database reachable only from approved inside services. Its firewall enforces which traffic may cross a boundary. A default-deny policy requires an explicit permission for new exposure; default allow requires an explicit restriction. Choosing the default determines what happens when a new service appears before a matching rule is written.

A packet filter compares protocol, source and destination IP addresses, source and destination ports, and any other configured fields with its rules. In a first-match policy, evaluate from the top and stop when a rule matches. Broad early rules can cover the same traffic as a later exception. If no explicit rule matches, apply the stated default. The exact processing semantics should be supplied in a rule problem.

A stateless filter decides from this packet and its rules. A stateful firewall records approved communication and checks later traffic against expected endpoints, protocol and state. A reply packet travels inward even when an inside client initiated the connection outward. Keep packet direction separate from connection initiation. Merely setting a TCP ACK flag is a weak substitute for validated connection state because an attacker can set header bits.

Port numbers are protocol conventions. Cooperative programs can put other data on a familiar port. Tunneling wraps inner traffic inside another protocol, such as carrying data in DNS messages. Deep packet inspection (DPI) examines payload structure as well as headers, using additional processing and protocol knowledge. Encryption limits inspection to what a middlebox can observe or legitimately decrypt. The chosen observation layer determines the available policy evidence.

A remote-access virtual private network (VPN) authenticates a remote peer and supplies a protected tunnel to a gateway. Access beyond that gateway still follows network and application policy. A compromised remote endpoint can use a valid tunnel, so endpoint trust matters. An application proxy terminates one application session and starts another, allowing application-aware checks at the proxy. Requiring that route is part of enforcing the policy.

Central enforcement simplifies consistent control, but the policy must match changing services and users. Restrictive boundaries reduce connectivity and can complicate peer-to-peer communication. Allowed traffic still reaches application code, and compromised inside systems may already occupy the trusted side. Firewall rules, host protection and application authorization therefore enforce different boundaries along the complete path.
example: With first-match processing, put “allow TCP from 203.0.113.8:any to 192.0.2.20:443” before “deny TCP from any to 192.0.2.20:443” to permit that one source. Reversing the rules makes the broad deny settle its packet first. A stateful return rule separately permits only replies belonging to an approved tracked connection.

questions.prompt: A first-match firewall has: (1) deny TCP from any to 192.0.2.20:443; (2) allow TCP from 203.0.113.8:any to that service; default deny. Evaluate a packet from 203.0.113.8:52000 and propose the smallest order change that expresses the exception.
questions.hint: Write the packet fields, then stop at the first matching rule.
questions.answer: Rule 1 matches, so the packet is denied before rule 2 is reached. Placing the narrow allow rule before the broad deny permits that source while retaining the deny for other sources. The result depends on the stated first-match semantics.

questions.prompt: A policy permits inside clients to start HTTPS connections. An HTTPS reply arrives inward. What information lets a stateful firewall treat it as an approved reply, and what limitation remains?
questions.hint: Separate packet direction, tracked connection endpoints and application content.
questions.answer: The firewall matches the packet to the recorded protocol/endpoints and expected connection state of the approved outbound flow. Its inward direction is consistent with a reply. The tracked state establishes permitted communication under that policy; application payload still needs its own security checks.

explanation: Availability means users can obtain a service when needed. A denial-of-service (DoS) attack interrupts that access through a flaw or by consuming a needed resource. Distributed DoS (DDoS) draws on many sending systems. A link, packet-processing engine, request queue, CPU or connection table can become the bottleneck. Identify the resource and its capacity before choosing a defense.

Let R be the counted bit rate in bits per second and L the counted bytes per packet. Packet rate is P = R/(8L) packets per second. A fixed bit rate generates more packet-handling work when packets are smaller. State which headers and link overhead are counted; mixing a payload-only size with a wire bit rate gives an inconsistent estimate. Fig. 2 lets the offered load and packet size change under an explicitly simplified resource model.

Filtering can discard traffic with known source or format patterns. Source spoofing forges an address; distribution adds actual senders. These complicate separating attack traffic from legitimate use. Filtering must occur while capacity remains: a host filter drops packets only after they have already crossed its access link. Source-address validation near sending networks reduces the set of addresses attackers can forge.

A TCP SYN flood can consume half-open connection state. A SYN-cookie server encodes recoverable setup information plus an integrity check into its SYN-ACK initial sequence number c, using a secret and freshness information. It keeps no ordinary per-SYN half-open record for that response. A completing client returns ACK = c+1; the server validates the returned information before allocating the established connection. A blind off-path sender with a forged source generally cannot observe the SYN-ACK needed to complete that proof. Cookie design, negotiated features and implementation details constrain the technique.

Reflection makes another server send the traffic. An attacker sends a UDP request whose source address is the victim’s address; the server sends its response to that claimed return address. A small DNS query can produce a larger answer, especially when the answer carries additional records or DNSSEC signatures. UDP request/response services can reply before proving return reachability, which makes blind source spoofing useful for this attack. The victim sees the responding servers’ addresses on those packets. Those addresses identify the reflectors; tracing the original sender requires additional evidence.

Let the counted response be Bᵣ bytes and request Bq bytes. Byte amplification is A = Bᵣ/Bq, so an attacker request rate r bit/s can induce approximately Ar bit/s of replies when the reflectors have capacity. One 80-byte request answered by one 1,200-byte response gives A = 15. If each fits in one unfragmented datagram, the datagram count remains one-for-one while the byte volume grows. Fig. 2 makes that distinction adjustable. Consistent byte accounting, fragmentation and the number of responses per request determine the actual totals. Closing unnecessary public responders, limiting response size or rate, and validating source addresses address different parts of the path.

A mitigation or content-delivery network can place a much larger shared pool of capacity in the service path. Consider a store whose ordinary server handles the usual traffic but fills its request queue during a flood. Its provider can distribute requests, add serving capacity and filter upstream, drawing on resources shared across many customers. This succeeds while usable link, packet-processing and application capacity exceed the remaining offered load. Each of those resources has its own limit. A SYN cookie protects a half-open state table; upstream capacity protects a different bottleneck.

A network telescope observes traffic reaching a range that should be quiet. For an IPv4 /p telescope, its fraction of the address space is f = 2^(32−p)/2^32 = 2^(−p). Under uniform independent source spoofing, one reply per triggering packet and no observation loss, a measured m replies/s estimates a total reply rate m/f. Here p is the prefix length, m counts identified backscatter replies, and the inferred rate uses the same response population. Filtering, uneven spoofing and different response counts change that inference.

The lower flow in Fig. 1 follows backscatter. A target replies to an attack packet’s randomly forged source address, and a quiet monitored address happens to receive that reply. Investigators group related replies using evidence such as the target address and protocol before extrapolating. Other observation designs can rotate monitored addresses or watch unused ports on otherwise active hosts. Each design needs a clear rule for which replies are unsolicited and a known sampling process. The simple 2^(−p) scaling above applies to the stated fixed address range and uniform-address model; another selection process needs its corresponding inclusion fraction.
example: A 24 Mbit/s counted stream using 600-byte packets has P = 24,000,000/(8 × 600) = 5,000 packets/s. Under matching byte accounting, reflectors answering each 80-byte request with 1,200 bytes give A = 15. A /10 telescope covers 1/1,024 of IPv4, so 90 identified backscatter replies/s estimate 92,160 total replies/s under the stated random-source, one-response and loss-free assumptions.

questions.prompt: An access link carries 12 Mbit/s of counted traffic. Compare 1,500-byte and 100-byte packets, ignoring additional overhead. Which count changes, and why might a SYN cookie still leave this link saturated?
questions.hint: Convert bytes to bits for each packet; then identify the resource protected by delayed state allocation.
questions.answer: The rates are 12,000,000/(8 × 1,500) = 1,000 packets/s and 12,000,000/(8 × 100) = 15,000 packets/s. Small packets create fifteen times as many handling events at the same bit rate. A SYN cookie protects half-open connection-state allocation; the incoming packets still consume access-link capacity.

questions.prompt: A /12 IPv4 telescope observes 35 identifiable backscatter replies per second. Estimate the total reply rate under uniform independent source spoofing, one response per triggering packet and no losses. Which assumption would a reflector attack with the fixed victim source violate?
questions.hint: Compute the telescope’s address fraction and identify where replies are addressed.
questions.answer: A /12 has fraction 1/4,096. The estimate is 35 × 4,096 = 143,360 replies/s. A reflection attack using one victim’s fixed source sends replies to that victim rather than uniformly scattered addresses, violating the uniform-source sampling assumption for this inference.

explanation: A virus arranges for copied code to execute later, often by infecting a stored program or document that someone opens. A worm automatically propagates to another vulnerable system and causes its new copy to run, allowing propagation to continue without a fresh user action at every hop. Real malware can combine methods. The important mechanism is how each new instance gets executed.

A worm needs a way to find a prospective victim and a way to make its code run there. Random address scanning can discover an exposed service; a search-based worm can use indexed pages to find a particular web platform. An exploit that achieves remote code execution makes the victim run code supplied from another system. Examples include a vulnerable network service or stored XSS that runs in another visitor’s browser. Discovering an address supplies a target. Successful execution creates the next propagator.

Parallel propagation creates rapid early growth: newly infected hosts join the scanning or delivery work. In a simple doubling model, I(t) = I₀ × 2^(t/d), where I₀ is the initial infected-host count, t elapsed time and d the doubling interval in the same units. This model assumes a sufficiently large reachable susceptible population and stable effective growth. Finite populations, duplicate targeting, patching, isolation and resource limits eventually change it. Fig. 2 explores the stated early-growth assumptions.

The Morris Worm combined multiple targeting and exploitation routes. Later, Code Red illustrates a gap between an available repair and a repaired system. It exploited a known buffer-overflow vulnerability in Microsoft IIS, after a patch had already been released. Exposed servers that remained vulnerable could still be compromised. The new copies could continue spreading and participate in other activity, including denial of service. Publishing a fix, deploying it and limiting exposure are separate steps in that story.

SQL Slammer made each new infection especially cheap: its exploit and worm code fit in a single UDP datagram aimed at a vulnerable database-related service. A sender could send another probe immediately, without a TCP handshake or a separate reply before moving on. Each newly infected machine joined that sending work. A telescope can receive worm exploit probes directly; their source is a scanning system, while a DoS backscatter packet comes from the responding attack target.

Reachability changes this process. An internal service behind a NAT gateway with no applicable inbound mapping or forwarding rule is harder for an outside scanner to reach. A stateful firewall can enforce which new inbound connections are allowed; patching removes the vulnerable behavior. Public servers and deliberately exposed ports remain reachable targets. These changes reduce the combination of reachable services and exploitable software on which a fast scanning worm depends.

A botnet is a collection of compromised machines under common attacker control. Its command-and-control (C2 or C&C) system distributes tasks and updates. Infection can come from a worm, malicious attachment, drive-by compromise or purchased access. Control can use a central server, a hierarchy or a peer-to-peer design. The compromise mechanism and the continuing control topology are distinct parts of the system.

A Host-based Intrusion Detection System (HIDS) can observe local files, processes, system calls and traffic, depending on its privileges and implementation. It requires host deployment and may itself be attacked after compromise. A Network Intrusion Detection System (NIDS) observes traffic at its network position, allowing centralized monitoring of visible flows. End-to-end encryption limits payload access there. Each sensor’s position defines the evidence it can collect; signatures, behavior models and evasion affect detection quality.

The lower panel of Fig. 1 separates three dependencies: find an endpoint, reach its service, and accept its commands. Removing a C2 IP interrupts one reachable server. Fast flux changes the IP addresses associated with a continuing name, so bots can resolve the name again. Seizing that name attacks the discovery step. A Domain Generation Algorithm (DGA) gives bots a changing collection of possible names to try; an operator may keep contact through a small working subset. A hosting or domain provider that resists abuse complaints is often called bulletproof, making a complaint-based takedown depend on that provider’s cooperation.

Command authentication remains its own step. A bot can carry the botmaster’s trusted public key and require a valid signature on each command. A defender who controls a rendezvous name can redirect queries or interrupt contact, while generating an accepted new command still requires the signing key or another compromise of that validation. This uses the same public-key verification mechanism studied earlier in the course.

Defenders can also work with upstream networks to disconnect a hosting service. That action targets connectivity for all infrastructure using the affected path; moving to another provider can restore the attacker’s contact route. Peer-to-peer C2 instead relays signed commands through compromised peers. It avoids reliance on one central command server, but intermittent peers and multiple forwarding steps can delay delivery. A preannounced coordinated action can tolerate propagation delay better than an immediate command.

Many individually small devices can become a substantial botnet resource when their traffic is combined. An IoT botnet connects the compromise and control story back to availability: the botmaster coordinates many senders against the same bottleneck. Patching, least privilege and endpoint isolation reduce compromise and spread; network controls restrict paths; host and network monitoring reveal activity; infrastructure action can interrupt control. Recovery still has to address the compromised hosts. Infection counts, active C2 contacts and reachable susceptible hosts measure different parts of this process.
example: Starting with 3 infected hosts and a 4-minute ideal doubling interval gives I(20) = 3 × 2^5 = 96 hosts after 20 minutes. This extrapolation requires enough susceptible reachable hosts and no limiting intervention. If defenders seize one rendezvous domain while bots generate alternative names and verify signed replies, they must examine both the alternate discovery path and the command-signature trust key.

questions.prompt: A worm starts at 5 hosts and doubles every 3 minutes in an ideal early-growth model. Find I after 18 minutes, then identify two environmental changes that would reduce confidence in continuing that curve.
questions.hint: Count complete doubling intervals; then inspect the supply of reachable vulnerable targets and the growth process.
questions.answer: There are 18/3 = 6 intervals, so I = 5 × 2^6 = 320 hosts. A shrinking susceptible population, duplicate scans, patching, isolation or saturated network resources can reduce effective growth. The model’s stable doubling rate would need to be re-estimated.

questions.prompt: Defenders seize a botnet’s usual rendezvous domain. Bots also try DGA names and verify commands with an embedded public key. Which continuing dependencies determine whether defenders can redirect or control the bots?
questions.hint: Separate finding a server from trusting its commands.
questions.answer: DGA names can provide alternative discovery routes after the usual name is seized. Command signatures require the private key corresponding to the embedded trusted public key, so controlling a name alone does not grant command-signing authority. Defenders must assess the remaining rendezvous routes, signature trust and recovery of compromised hosts.
